Actually, thinking about it more, I think there might be a simpler approach. The `$` anchor in Python regex matches at the end of the string OR just before a newline at the end of the string. This means that when you have `^...$` with `DOTALL`:

- `'hello\n'` → `$` matches at position 5 (before `\n`)
- `'hello\n\n'` → `$` matches at position 6 (before the last `\n`)

So if we have `^hello (.+?)$` and the string is `'hello world\n\n'`:
- `^` matches at 0
- `hello ` matches positions 0-5
- `.+?` lazily matches from position 6
- `$` must match at some position
- `$` potentially matches at position 11 (before the first `\n`), position 12 (before the second `\n`), or position 13 (end of string)
- Since `$` matches before the last newline, it matches at position 12
- So `.+?` must match from 6 to 12 = `'world\n'`

This is technically correct regex behavior, but the user might expect `'world'`.

One approach to fix this: in the `parse` method, we could strip trailing whitespace (or just trailing newlines) from the string before matching. But this could break cases where the format explicitly includes a trailing newline and the caller expects it to be consumed by the format, not by the stripping.
